source: Gutierrez et al. (2025) From RAG to Memory: HippoRAG 2 (QA table)
finding: Graph-augmented retrieval (HippoRAG 2) beats the best flat embedding retriever on average QA F1, but only by a few points. The older HippoRAG loses to flat retrieval on several sets.
numbers: Llama-3.3-70B reader, NV-Embed-v2 retriever. Average F1 over seven sets: NV-Embed-v2 57.0, HippoRAG 2 59.8, HippoRAG 1 53.1, GraphRAG 49.6, RAPTOR 48.8, LightRAG 6.6. HotpotQA F1: NV-Embed-v2 75.3, HippoRAG 2 75.5, HippoRAG 1 63.5. Text: HippoRAG 2 beats NV-Embed-v2 by 9.5% F1 on 2Wiki and 3.1% on LV-Eval. Bootstrap p<0.05 marked vs NV-Embed-v2.
limits: Table cells were garbled by PDF extraction; only values I could align with row labels are listed. Authors say large flat embedders beat graph methods on simple QA.
agent_relevance: Graph memory gives a few points on multi-hop and loses on simple lookup. Keep flat retrieval as default and add a graph path only for multi-hop chains.

finding: Recall shows the graph gain mainly on 2Wiki and MuSiQue. HotpotQA is near ceiling for both. HippoRAG 2 no longer loses on HotpotQA, unlike HippoRAG 1.
numbers: Recall@5, NV-Embed-v2 vs HippoRAG 2: NQ 75.4 vs 78.0; PopQA 51.0 vs 51.7; MuSiQue 69.7 vs 74.7; 2Wiki 76.5 vs 90.4; HotpotQA 94.5 vs 96.3. HippoRAG 1 (reproduced): 53.2 / 90.4 / 77.3 on MuSiQue / 2Wiki / HotpotQA. Ablations in the paper show linking by whole query instead of extracted phrases and removing passage nodes both lower recall (avg 74.6 and 59.6 vs 87.1 as aligned).
limits: Ablation row labels are misaligned in the extracted table; treat the ablation averages as approximate. This is recall, not final answer quality.
agent_relevance: Gap 1: the HotpotQA loss belongs to HippoRAG 1. The gain depends on design details (passage nodes, phrase-level linking), not on graph structure alone.

source: Gutierrez et al. (2025) HippoRAG 2 (cost, Appendix F, Table 12)
finding: Building the graph costs many more tokens than plain embedding, but HippoRAG 2 is much cheaper to build than GraphRAG or LightRAG.
numbers: MuSiQue corpus, 11,656 passages. Indexing input tokens: NV-Embed-v2 none; RAPTOR 1.7M; HippoRAG 1 and 2 9.2M; LightRAG 68.5M; GraphRAG 115.5M. Output tokens: HippoRAG 3.0M, LightRAG 18.3M, GraphRAG 36.1M, RAPTOR 0.2M. QA time per query: NV-Embed-v2 12.1 s, HippoRAG 2 99.5 s, GraphRAG 277 s. GPU memory: NV-Embed 0.3 GB, HippoRAG 2 1.2 GB.
limits: Authors say all graph methods lag plain RAG on time and memory. The earlier 10-30x cheaper claim is relative to iterative retrieval, a different baseline.
agent_relevance: Gap 10: graph building is a fixed cost of about 12M tokens per 11k passages with no flat equivalent. Worth it only for a large, long-lived memory.

source: Han et al. (2025/2026) RAG vs. GraphRAG: A Systematic Evaluation (QA tables)
finding: Under one unified protocol, flat RAG wins on single-hop detail questions. Graph methods win only on multi-hop, temporal and comparison questions.
numbers: Llama-3.1-8B. NQ F1: RAG 64.78, HippoRAG2 61.03, Community-GraphRAG(Local) 63.01, KG-GraphRAG 34.28 to 50.27. HotpotQA F1: RAG 60.04, HippoRAG2 63.01, Local 61.66. MultiHop-RAG overall: RAG 67.02, Local 69.01, RAPTOR 68.78. Temporal: RAG 30.70 vs Local 50.60. Null: RAG 96.01 vs Local 80.07.
limits: Mainly one reader family. Overall gains are 2-3 points; the graph advantage sits in temporal and comparison query types.
agent_relevance: Gap 1: task-dependent. Route by query type; do not make graph retrieval the default.

source: Han et al. (2025/2026) RAG vs. GraphRAG (token-matched control, Appendix M)
finding: When flat RAG gets the same input tokens as GraphRAG, the overall graph advantage disappears. Only temporal questions keep a clear edge.
numbers: MultiHop-RAG, Llama-3.1-8B. RAG 67.02 overall; RAG with matched tokens 69.33; Community-GraphRAG(Local) 69.01. Temporal: matched RAG 36.71 vs Local 50.60 (about 14 points). Comparison: 59.81 vs 60.63.
quote: does lead to slight performance gains, our main conclusions remain unchanged
limits: Only the MultiHop-RAG matched table was read; the other datasets (Tables 33-35) were not. The row assignment of the matched row is inferred from table order.
agent_relevance: Gap 1 at equal tokens: the overall win is erased. Spend tokens on more flat chunks unless the query is temporal or comparative.

source: Han et al. (2025/2026) RAG vs. GraphRAG (graph coverage failure)
finding: An LLM-built graph misses answer content, which caps graph-only retrieval.
numbers: Only about 65.8% of answer entities appear in the constructed KG for HotpotQA and 65.5% for NQ. KG-GraphRAG with triplets only: HotpotQA F1 25.02 vs 60.04 for RAG.
limits: Applies to LLM-extracted entity graphs, not to graphs from structured sources.
agent_relevance: Keep raw text next to graph edges in agent memory; edges alone lose about a third of the answers.

source: Han et al. (2025/2026) RAG vs. GraphRAG (reranking and iterative retrieval)
finding: Reranking and iterative retrieval (IRCoT) help flat and graph methods alike, more so on multi-hop.
numbers: On NQ and MultiHop-RAG, all methods improved; under these strategies GraphRAG methods typically beat RAG on MultiHop-RAG. Community-GraphRAG(Local)+IRCoT was weak on Null queries.
limits: Exact deltas are in a figure I did not extract.
agent_relevance: Gap 1 and 5: an iterative loop is a competing use of the same tokens. No test of a deliberate explore/exploit mix was found.

source: Xiang et al. (2026) When to Use Graphs in RAG (GraphRAG-Bench, ICLR 2026)
finding: Across four task levels, flat RAG matches or beats graph methods on simple fact retrieval. Graph methods help more on complex reasoning, summarisation and creative generation.
numbers: Seven GraphRAG systems vs RAG with and without rerank, GPT-4o-mini, novel and medical corpora. Authors: Obs.1 basic RAG comparable or better on simple facts; Obs.2 GraphRAG clear advantage on complex reasoning, summarise and creative generation; Obs.5 advantage grows with question difficulty. Cell values in the extracted tables were not reliable, so none are quoted.
limits: Two domains only (novels, medical). Conclusions are the authors' stated observations.
agent_relevance: Gap 1: independent support that benefit tracks task complexity. Creative generation is the closest proxy for analogue use.

source: Xiang et al. (2026) GraphRAG-Bench (token cost and graph statistics)
finding: Graph retrieval often multiplies prompt size. HippoRAG 2 is the exception.
numbers: Average prompt tokens, novel/medical: vanilla RAG 879/954; HippoRAG2 1,008/1,020; HippoRAG 7,208/7,342; RAPTOR 3,441/3,510; Fast-GraphRAG 4,204/4,298; MS-GraphRAG local 38,707/39,821; global 331,375/332,881; LightRAG 100,832/100,310. Index graphs are sparse: average degree about 1.5 to 13 and clustering coefficient about 0.09 to 0.66 depending on system.
limits: Query-time prompt tokens only, not build cost. Graph statistics vary strongly by implementation.
agent_relevance: Gap 10 and 6: query cost can be near flat (+15%) or 100x. LLM-built memory graphs are sparse, so the hub centralisation seen in literature graphs is not shown here.

finding: On LoCoMo a flat extracted-memory store gets most of the full-context score at about 7% of the tokens. Adding a graph (Mem0g) adds 1.6 points at twice the tokens.
numbers: Overall LLM-judge J: full-context 72.90 (26,031 tokens); Mem0g 68.44 (3,616); Mem0 66.88 (1,764); Zep 65.99 (3,911); LangMem 58.10 (127); best fixed-chunk RAG about 61; OpenAI memory 52.90 (4,437); A-Mem re-run 48.38 (2,520).
limits: Vendor paper; baselines re-run by the authors (A-Mem number is their re-run). LoCoMo conversations are about 26k tokens so full context fits.
agent_relevance: Gap 1, 8, 10: flat memory is the cost-efficient default; the graph variant adds little per token.

source: Chhikara et al. (2025) Mem0 (by question type)
finding: The graph variant helps temporal questions. On single-hop and multi-hop it gives no gain.
numbers: Temporal: Mem0g F1 51.55, J 58.13; Mem0 J 55.51. Multi-hop: Mem0 F1 28.64, J 51.15, graph memory gave no gain. Single-hop: graph adds little. Open-domain J: Zep 76.60, Mem0g 75.71, Mem0 72.93.
limits: One vendor-run evaluation; no variance across seeds seen in the text I read.
agent_relevance: Gap 1: multi-hop integration, the use closest to analogue chaining, was not helped by graph edges here. Timestamps and ordering were the real value.

source: Rasmussen et al. (2025) Zep: A Temporal Knowledge Graph Architecture for Agent Memory
finding: A temporal graph memory beats full context on LongMemEval in accuracy and cuts latency about 90%, but loses on some single-session types.
numbers: LongMemEval-s: gpt-4o-mini full-context 55.4% (115k tokens) vs Zep 63.8% (1.6k tokens); gpt-4o 60.2% vs 71.2%. Latency 31.3 s to 3.20 s (mini). gpt-4o by type: temporal 45.1 to 62.4; multi-session 44.3 to 57.9; single-session-assistant 94.6 to 80.4. DMR: Zep 94.8%, full conversation 94.4%, MemGPT 93.4% (gpt-4-turbo).
limits: Zep authors' own evaluation. No flat-vector baseline between full context and Zep, so graph and compression effects are confounded. MemGPT could not be run on LongMemEval.
agent_relevance: Gap 1 and 10: 1.6k tokens of retrieved memory beats 115k of raw history, but the paper cannot say the graph caused it.

source: Si, Hashimoto, Yang (2025) The Ideation-Execution Gap
finding: The novelty advantage of LLM ideas did not survive execution. LLM idea scores dropped 1 to 2 points; human ideas did not drop.
numbers: 43 experts each spent over 100 hours executing 24 AI and 19 human ideas across 7 NLP topics; 181 reviews. Ideation scores AI vs human: novelty 5.778 vs 4.912, excitement 5.653 vs 4.404, effectiveness 6.003 vs 4.833, overall 5.382 vs 4.596. Change after execution: human -0.010, +0.078, -0.052; AI -1.049 (novelty), -1.760 (excitement), -1.879 (effectiveness). Execution scores: excitement 3.90 (AI) vs 4.48, effectiveness 4.13 vs 4.78; per-idea difference not significant at N=43.
limits: NLP prompting ideas only; one idea generator. Executors changed some ideas (for example removed non-existent datasets).
agent_relevance: Gap 9: the novelty gain does not carry to executed outcomes in the same domain. No replication outside NLP found. Do not rank ideas by novelty rating alone.

source: Si, Hashimoto, Yang (2025) Ideation-Execution Gap (ideation vs execution correlation)
finding: Pre-execution review scores barely predict post-execution scores.
numbers: Appendix D, Table 9: correlations between ideation and execution scores are weak in most cases; for AI ideas the excitement score correlates moderately negatively. In the execution reviews, overall score and effectiveness correlate r=0.654.
limits: Exact coefficients were not read from the garbled table.
agent_relevance: Gap 3: a review-style score of a new idea is not a cheap proxy for usefulness. A feasibility-grounded check is needed, and none was found that works without execution.

source: Wen et al. (2025) Predicting Empirical AI Research Outcomes with Language Models
finding: Predicting which of two ideas works is near chance for off-the-shelf frontier models. A fine-tuned model with paper retrieval beats experts.
numbers: 1,585 test pairs, 6,000 training pairs. Fine-tuned GPT-4.1 plus retrieval: 77% overall; 64.4% vs 48.9% for 25 human experts on NLP; ceiling human baseline 60.0%; inter-annotator agreement 75.1%. o3 and other frontier models near random even with retrieval. On unpublished ideas including AI-generated ones: 63.6%.
limits: Pairwise comparison of published-style ideas; transfer to an agent's own free-form ideas is only 63.6%.
agent_relevance: Gap 4: self-ranking by a general model is near chance. External grounding plus training helps; without training expect about the 53% level.

source: Wen et al. (2025) Predicting Empirical AI Research Outcomes (what grounding adds)
finding: Retrieved papers lift accuracy; fine-tuning on past outcomes lifts it more.
numbers: Paper retrieval raised accuracy from 38.8% to 53.0% (Table 3 text); abstracts alone biased the model toward old ideas. Fine-tuning GPT-4.1 on past ideas moved it from 51.9% to 77%. Fine-tuning GPT-3.5-turbo moved it from 45.0% to 53.7% (earlier cutoff).
limits: Fine-tuning is training, which our scaffold excludes. Retrieval baseline of 38.8% is below chance, so part of the lift is removing a bias.
agent_relevance: Gap 4: retrieval of related results is a legal scaffold move worth about +14 points from a below-chance start; it does not reach the trained level.
